title: Korach: Moses falls on his face (Numbers 16:4)
hookLine: attacked, Moses first falls on his face before answering
tomorrow: Korach: the man who went home

cards: The message arrives at 11pm. It's sharp, it's public, and half of it is unfair. Thumbs start moving before the mind catches up, and a reply sent in that moment can look very different by morning.
In the Torah, Korach and two hundred and fifty leaders of the community gather against Moses and Aaron and accuse them, to their faces, of lifting themselves above everyone else.
It's an attack on Moses' whole life's work. Everyone waits for his answer. Before he says a single word, he does something else.

teach.b: The verse is very short. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face." In Hebrew, va-yipol al panav.
He drops to the ground, face down, in front of the crowd. The Torah doesn't explain why, and the commentators fill the silence in different ways.
Rashi, the great medieval commentator, reads it as distress: this was not the first time the people had turned on him, and Moses felt he had little left to say on their behalf.
Others read it as prayer, a way of turning to God before turning to the people. Either way, notice the order. First he falls silent.
Then he speaks. And when he speaks, he doesn't answer the insult. He says, in paraphrase, in the morning the Lord will show who is His.
In the morning: he gives the night a chance.

teach.h: IN THE MORNING: TIME TO THINK AGAIN.
teach.b: Rashi suggests Moses hoped that with a few hours, they might think again. Then Moses sends for two of the leading rebels, Dathan and Abiram, to talk. They refuse to come.

teach.h: HIS FIRST MOVE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: Moses falls on his face again and again in the book of Numbers: when the people despair after the scouts' report, and twice more during this very rebellion, pleading for the people's lives.
It becomes a pattern when things fall apart. Not a weapon. A pause, with his face to the ground, before anything else.

how: In traditional weekday prayer, a short section called tachanun is said with the head resting on the arm, and its traditional name, nefilat apayim, falling on the face, echoes the way Moses and Aaron fell on their faces in the wilderness.

o: the rebellion that brought Moses to his face
the morning offering of incense at the altar
a bow made in prayer each weekday morning

games.q: what happened, in order of the story — tap the pairs.
p: the Lord will show who is His

s: the Torah explains why Moses fell on his face
it doesn't. commentators read it as distress, as prayer, or both.
Moses falls on his face more than once in Numbers
after the spies' report, and more than once during Korach's rebellion.
Moses answered by defending his own record
he answered that in the morning the Lord would show who is His.

games.q: you're Moses. a crowd of leaders accuses you, publicly, of grabbing power. what's your first move?
o: answer every charge on the spot.
fall on your face, then speak.
walk away and say nothing at all.
games.why: he fell on his face, then spoke, and even then he put the decision off until morning, giving everyone a night to think again.

practice: Lower your eyes or close them, and bring to mind a time someone came at you with words, last week or years ago; notice how fast the answer wanted to come.
Instead of answering, let your head bow a little, and let the reply wait while you breathe. If a better answer comes, keep it for later.

wordCard.voice: Korach. The rebellion that brought Moses to the ground before it brought him to his feet, falling on his face first, then answering.

orig.note: Hebrew: and he fell on his face, Moses' first response to Korach (Numbers 16:4).

carryVoice: Your line: fall silent first. His answer could wait until morning, and so can yours. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face.
